articles.title: Jump in energy bills drives UK inflation to highest rate for four months
articles.summary: The cost of things is now rising at a faster pace compared with last month.
articles.content:
Higher energy bills drove UK inflation up to 2.9% in the 12 months to July, the latest figures show.

Energy costs rose on 1 July after regulator Ofgem increased the price cap on household gas and electricity bills by 13%, which added £221 a year to the typical household's bill.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the increase to the energy price cap was driven by "the largest rise in gas prices for almost four years".

The July increase is the highest rate of inflation since March, when it was 3.3%.

ONS prices director Mike Hardie said furniture prices, which fell by less than usual for that time of year, added to the upward pressure on inflation, and said clothing was also not being discounted as much.

Chancellor John Healey said the Iran war was continuing to affect prices in the UK, but insisted Britain's economy was resilient.

"We have cut VAT on electricity bills and capped bus fares at £2 - to give breathing space to those feeling the strain," he said.

"There is more to do to restore hope and build a stronger economy where prosperity is shared more fairly across Britain."

KPMG's chief economist Yael Selfin said July marked the start of a gradual rise in inflation, though she said Wednesday's figure was not enough to spur change in the Bank of England's interest-rate setting decisions.

But Selfin added that energy-related costs were expected to push inflation higher over the coming months to a peak of about 3.5%.

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said the country was unprepared for global shocks due to Labour's "mismanagement", leaving ordinary people "paying the price".

Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here

articles.title: Rare cows part of estate's rewilding project
articles.summary: White Park cattle arrive at the Castle Howard estate in North Yorkshire to support conservation.
articles.content:
A rare breed of cattle has been introduced to the grounds of a historic house in North Yorkshire as part of a 30-year conservation project.

The arrival of the White Park cows, thought to be one of the most ancient species of its kind, is the latest phase of the Bog Hall rewilding scheme on the Castle Howard Estate, near Malton.

Their grazing in the newly-sown meadows would "help create a more varied habitat structure", the estate said.

Head of natural environment, Guy Thallon, said reintroducing animals had been "inspiring for the whole Castle Howard team and beyond", with further plans to release beavers in the autumn.

Approximately three miles (5km) of fencing has been installed ahead of their release, with badger tunnels and otter passes built to maintain safe routes for wildlife.

"The conservation volunteers have been preparing the site by creating ponds and planting willow," Thallon said.

"We can't wait to see the positive impact of nature's engineers in the coming years."

The rewilding project covers 440 acres within the Howardian Hills National Landscape

Meanwhile, the cows have taken up residence in the project area, where they will live outside all year round.

The herd was chosen because it is suited to "outdoor conservation grazing, including in wetter grassland habitats", the estate added.

It is priority-listed by the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, which describes it as "likely the most ancient native cattle in the British Isles".

The Bog Hall Habitat Bank project hopes to restore and rewild 440 acres of agricultural land into a "thriving space for nature", the estate said.

Part of the area, which sits within the Howardian Hills National Landscape, is designated as a Site of Importance for Nature Conservation.

The project is being delivered in partnership with biodiversity research organisation Environment Bank.

Guy Thallon says it was "exciting" to see the cattle exploring their new home

The scheme began in 2024 and volunteers have so far restored meadows and created scrub banks to protect saplings.

Ponds and leaky dams have also been installed to hold more water across the site.

Thallon said children from nearby primary schools had designed signage for the fencing around the area, featuring "animals they would like to see in the Bog Hall Habitat Bank project in the future".

Fraser Rutherford, head of marketing at Environment Bank, said for pupils, it was a "rare opportunity to follow nature restoration throughout their school years and see firsthand how native wildlife returns to a landscape".

articles.content:
I found two days of hard graft – repairing hiking paths with a conservation trust in stunningly remote Wester Ross – a surprisingly rewarding experience

I hadn’t planned to enjoy any of this. As summer light fell on Stac Pollaidh – the summit’s teeth bared, the views stretching across the surreal emptiness of Assynt – I found myself ankle-deep in blanket bog next to a hiking path, back bent, hacking at the tough terrain with a heavy-duty mattock. Farther up the hillside, another hunched figure was cutting a deep brown scar into the moor grass and, while he worked, I stood back to look at my efforts. At my feet was a cross drain that I’d unblocked and repacked with new stonework to prevent storm damage and aid runoff from the path. A burble began to trickle, slow yet clear across the sparkling bedrock. It felt a little like appreciating a masterwork in a museum.

I’d come to Wester Ross with a bucket and spade, not for a beach break at particularly gorgeous Achmelvich or Clachtoll nearby, but with the notion of giving something back to the hills. The Outdoor Access Trust for Scotland (Oats) is a steward of many of the Highlands’ most famous mountains – developing, building and repairing paths and habitats – and I’d joined a group of volunteers for a two-day stint on the north-west Highlands’ most visited peak. Factoring in a free stay at Ullapool youth hostel and the promise of a home-cooked communal meal in return, plus an acceptable midge-free forecast, I’d driven north from Edinburgh the night before in a buoyant mood.

Oats’s purpose is to promote sustainable public access and these days that’s largely done through voluntourism, with helpers set to work lifting, resurfacing and filling pathways, yielding landscape-scale results. Iconic if traffic-heavy mountains such as An Teallach, Lochnagar and Braeriach are annual priorities, as are a throng of glens and estates from Skye to the Cairngorms. (Due to this summer’s devastating fires, some events in the north Cairngorms may be changed to a different location or postponed.) The trust’s volunteers even regularly get to work on the Lairig Ghru, arguably Britain’s most unforgiving mountain pass.

It might sound like all hard graft, but it’s not. Volunteers learn new practical skills and gain awareness of mountain path design and the causes of erosion – mostly a combination of human misuse and increasing extreme weather conditions – in settings with extraordinary views. No experience is required, but volunteers must be used to spending time outdoors, have good physical fitness and be capable of using hand tools.

We started that first morning from Stac Pollaidh’s car park, a space transformed by Oats two years ago to accommodate four times more vehicles – a result of the mountain’s accessibility from the North Coast 500, which hurtles past (from Kylesku to Ullapool) only five miles east, at the end of the road. But everyone comes with the same motivation. As we climbed the open moorland, Assynt’s surrounding sea of lochans (small lochs) sparkled. Stac Pollaidh’s summit, to the north, appeared even more welcoming with its porcupine ridge under a sky as blue as a newborn’s eye.

From below the hilltop to the lower forest’s edge, we worked the path – unclogging ditches, removing invasive grasses, dredging, stabilising the soil, repacking stone drains, replanting edges – all while the mountain came to life. Trail runners, dog walkers and hikers from across Europe weaved up the slopes, stopping to ask what we were doing. A French school group trooped past, the pupils plastered with blue Braveheart face paint. A Dutch couple stopped to offer biscuits. Everyone swallowed the stunning views of Suilven to the north.

Our group of seven volunteers – including two New Zealanders; three retirees, one from Inverness, one from Stirling and another from Forfar; and an Edinburgh IT worker using his annual corporate volunteer days – appreciated the smiles.

To a newcomer, the Highlands’ mountain paths may appear to have always been there, as if part of the landscape’s DNA. But as Oats’s volunteer coordinator Eva Kupska said, they are “always evolving and always at risk from erosion, because of the influences of nature and man … and it is our job to conserve them”.

Every volunteer is vital. Post-Brexit, with a lack of EU funding streams, Eva told me there is a drastic need for a public fund for path maintenance and habitat restoration, and the charity simply doesn’t have the manpower to tackle the deteriorating pathways or native tree planting alone. To complicate matters, some of the most popular mountain paths are on privately owned land, with no access to any public funding.

There are a further 12 one-day, plus three- and five-day, maintenance and conservation events scheduled to take place this year, including some dedicated tree-planting trips. It’s a joyful shared experience. That first afternoon, flasks of hot tea were unscrewed and homemade fruit loaf was shared. There was the warm smell of flowering heather and the earthy stink of the bogs, along with the satisfaction of time well spent in the wild.

That evening, back in Ullapool, the harbour abuzz with tourists eating fish suppers and gulls circling above the trawlers, we stood in the sea-view kitchen of Ullapool youth hostel sharing life stories and the day’s experience. There are plenty of excellent dinner options, including The Seafood Shack and The Dipping Lugger , but we settled on a night of each other’s company (delightful), local beers (necessary) and a giant gurgling stockpot of Eva’s courgette and tomato risotto (terrific). And boy, did I sleep well.

The next day brought a gossamer mist to the hills of Wester Ross. We arrived earlier, picked up where we’d left off and, largely, never complained as the sun slowly cracked through the clouds. But best of all was seeing our progress as we worked down the mountain, step by step, always avoiding the fragile vegetation at the path’s edges, creating something better and more sustainable for tomorrow. A staycation with a purpose – and it felt good.

articles.content:
I was living on my own for the first time in 35 years, walking every day. Nature reminded me how much there still is to be found in emptiness

A fter my husband died, the birds started behaving strangely towards me. This was not my imagination; it really happened. On my daily walks, I was startled by how close they came to me – approaching, hopping alongside me and chirping. If there were a lot of them – and if there was no one else around – it felt as if they were accompanying me, maybe trying to convey something.

I had walked on the heath near our home with my husband for years. But his illness meant that, during his final months, he could not walk with me any more. When he died – in January 2023 – I had been walking on my own for six months and the birds, I am sure of this, had paid no attention to me.

Of course, it occurred to me that this might be a message from my husband. When you are newly bereaved, it’s easy to grasp at any sign that your loved one might somehow still be there. But, in the case of my husband, I knew this could not be. Firstly, he had told me before he died that he was certain there was no afterlife and it was totally irrational of me to think that there might be. Secondly, he would never ever have chosen to come back as a bird. He was a big man, who admired big powerful animals, and – if he was that way inclined – he might have come back as a tall, many-antlered stag, roaring at me from a misty mountainside. Or, maybe more likely, because he could be morose, he might have come back as a moose or an elk, lumbering out of a gloomy forest at dusk.

One evening, a robin followed me home. I know that robins often interact with people, perching on gardeners’ spades, making eye contact. But this robin hopped along beside me for an unusually long time, watching and apparently accompanying me. In a moment of foolishness, I stopped and said quietly to the bird: “OK, if it’s you, follow me home” and at once it flew away in a big fluttering rush.

Three months after my husband’s death, I went to France, to a small village in the foothills of the Alps. One evening, as I was climbing the outside stone staircase to my room, a young magpie appeared out of nowhere and perched on the banister beside me, making a tremendous fuss. He squawked and flapped his wings and bounced up and down, obviously beside himself. As he was less than two feet away from me, this was quite disconcerting. I still don’t know what was upsetting him but I do know that things like that never used to happen to me.

It made me begin to pay much more attention to my natural surroundings than I had before. I discovered the uncomplicated pleasure to be found in a weirdly shaped mushroom, in the steady clicking noise made by gorse bushes when the sun shines on them. I was not skipping through the woods, tra-la-la; I was far too sad. But my need to walk every day – which I have always had – acquired a new and deeper meaning.

Everywhere I went that first year, I looked for solace in nature. I had to keep moving, whether walking on the heath or leaving home to travel. It was in the stillness of staying put that the pain was worst.

Over time, I came to see that when you walk in nature with the person you love, you observe it, you enjoy it, but you are – to a certain extent – apart from it. Your companionship is its own universe. When you walk alone, you become more fully part of the world around you. So, no doubt, I was paying more attention to the birds. But I also think they sensed that there was something wrong with me – I was a wounded creature – and maybe they really were accompanying me.

Back home, there is another robin who regularly tries to catch my attention through the glass of the garden door. In the afternoons, an urban fox, always the same one – I know him from the scar on his forehead – snoozes in my garden. On many evenings, a mouse runs across the garden path at 8.30pm – always in the same direction – while, overhead, through the urban dusk, flocks of green parakeets head home along their known routes, traced in the sky. Nature reminds me continually how much there still is to be found in emptiness.

I relate to the natural world differently now that I have learned to sense it as company. I do still enjoy the companionship of people but with creatures there is no need for pretence. On the most active night of the Perseid meteor shower, I got up at three in the morning and saw three shooting stars from my open bedroom window. The next day, someone told me it was a good omen – but I knew that it was nothing of the sort. It just was.

This might all sound very fanciful, but it is these moments that have coloured my experience of living alone for the first time in 35 years. Still, as I walk in the woods, sometimes I imagine my husband laughing and rolling his eyes at how I told everyone that, after he died, the birds started behaving strangely towards me.

He was a big man, who admired big powerful animals, and – if he was that way inclined – he might have come back as a tall, many-antlered stag, roaring at me from a misty mountainside. Or, maybe more likely, because he could be morose, he might have come back as a moose or an elk, lumbering out of a gloomy forest at dusk.

One evening, a robin followed me home. I know that robins often interact with people, perching on gardeners’ spades, making eye contact. But this robin hopped along beside me for an unusually long time, watching and apparently accompanying me. In a moment of foolishness, I stopped and said quietly to the bird: “OK, if it’s you, follow me home” and at once it flew away in a big fluttering rush.

Three months after my husband’s death, I went to France, to a small village in the foothills of the Alps. One evening, as I was climbing the outside stone staircase to my room, a young magpie appeared out of nowhere and perched on the banister beside me, making a tremendous fuss. He squawked and flapped his wings and bounced up and down, obviously beside himself. As he was less than two feet away from me, this was quite disconcerting. I still don’t know what was upsetting him but I do know that things like that never used to happen to me.

It made me begin to pay much more attention to my natural surroundings than I had before. I discovered the uncomplicated pleasure to be found in a weirdly shaped mushroom, in the steady clicking noise made by gorse bushes when the sun shines on them. I was not skipping through the woods, tra-la-la; I was far too sad. But my need to walk every day – which I have always had – acquired a new and deeper meaning.

Everywhere I went that first year, I looked for solace in nature. I had to keep moving, whether walking on the heath or leaving home to travel. It was in the stillness of staying put that the pain was worst.

Over time, I came to see that when you walk in nature with the person you love, you observe it, you enjoy it, but you are – to a certain extent – apart from it. Your companionship is its own universe. When you walk alone, you become more fully part of the world around you. So, no doubt, I was paying more attention to the birds. But I also think they sensed that there was something wrong with me – I was a wounded creature – and maybe they really were accompanying me.

Back home, there is another robin who regularly tries to catch my attention through the glass of the garden door. In the afternoons, an urban fox, always the same one – I know him from the scar on his forehead – snoozes in my garden. On many evenings, a mouse runs across the garden path at 8.30pm – always in the same direction – while, overhead, through the urban dusk, flocks of green parakeets head home along their known routes, traced in the sky. Nature reminds me continually how much there still is to be found in emptiness.

I relate to the natural world differently now that I have learned to sense it as company. I do still enjoy the companionship of people but with creatures there is no need for pretence. On the most active night of the Perseid meteor shower, I got up at three in the morning and saw three shooting stars from my open bedroom window. The next day, someone told me it was a good omen – but I knew that it was nothing of the sort. It just was.

This might all sound very fanciful, but it is these moments that have coloured my experience of living alone for the first time in 35 years. Still, as I walk in the woods, sometimes I imagine my husband laughing and rolling his eyes at how I told everyone that, after he died, the birds started behaving strangely towards me.

articles.title: Jammy tomato risotto and amaretto roast peaches: Toklas chef Chris Shaw’s simple summer recipes
articles.summary: Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert At Toklas, ingredients such as datterini tomatoes and ripe peaches are taking centre stage. articles.content:
Make the most of the season’s freshest produce with a light but richly flavoured tomato-dosed dinner and a booze-laced, New York-inspired dessert

A t Toklas, ingredients such as datterini tomatoes and ripe peaches are taking centre stage. These recipes celebrate the simplicity of summer cooking, allowing produce to shine with minimal intervention. From a risotto layered with sweet tomatoes, pecorino and mint to roast peaches finished with amaretto and mascarpone, they capture the character of the season – fresh, generous and full of flavour.

A really light risotto. There’s no butter in it – just olive oil and cheese – and the richness comes predominantly from the roast tomatoes.

For the stock 4 shallots , peeled 2 sticks celery , trimmed 1 vine of tomatoes 2 carrots

For the roast tomatoes 500g datterini tomatoes , washed Salt Olive oil 4 garlic cloves, peeled For the risotto Olive oil 2 shallots , peeled and finely diced 1 garlic clove , peeled and crushed Salt and black pepper 350g risotto rice 2 tbsp tomato puree 150g pecorino romano , grated 30g fresh mint , leaves picked and finely chopped

To make the stock, roughly chop all the vegetables and put them in a saucepan. Cover with two litres of cold water and bring to boil over a high heat. Turn down the heat and leave to simmer for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat the oven to 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½. Put the tomatoes in a roasting tray, season with salt and drizzle with olive oil. Add the garlic, then roast for about an hour, until the tomatoes are jammy.

Bring a large, heavy-based pan to a medium heat. Add a generous glug of olive oil, followed by the diced shallots, crushed garlic and a pinch of salt. Once the shallots are soft, add the rice and stir well to coat. Add another pinch of salt then toast the rice for a minute or two, until the edges begin to look translucent. Add the tomato puree and cook for two to three minutes.

Strain the stock and discard the vegetable solids. Add the stock to the rice one large ladleful at a time, stirring continuously and allowing each addition to be absorbed before adding the next.

After about 18-20 minutes, when the rice is just cooked but still has a little bite, take the pan off the heat and stir through the roast tomatoes, roast garlic, grated pecorino and chopped mint. The tomatoes should break up nicely once incorporated into the hot rice.

Season to taste, finish with a generous glug of olive oil, if desired, and serve immediately.

Inspired by the restaurant Via Carota in New York , this is a really great summer dessert – it’s super-easy, too.

For the mascarpone cream 250g mascarpone 50ml double cream ¼ vanilla pod , seeds scraped out 50g icing sugar

For the peaches 4 good-quality (ideally yellow) peaches 75g icing sugar 150ml amaretto

Combine all the ingredients for the mascarpone cream in a bowl, beat well with a spatula until smooth, then chill until needed. (The cream helps soften the mascarpone, which can otherwise be quite stiff and heavy.)

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 . Halve the peaches, remove the stones, then cut each half in two. Arrange the peach quarters skin side down in a roasting tray. Using a sieve, dust evenly with the icing sugar, then pour the amaretto into the tray and roast for about 15 minutes, or until the peaches are tender and lightly caramelised.

Serve the warm peaches with the roasting juices spooned over and the mascarpone cream on the side.

articles.title: Nestory Irankunda says Pauline Hanson’s Socceroos monocultural claim made ‘us boys angry’
articles.summary: Forward says One Nation leader’s comments made him ‘emotional’ Players upset ‘because there’s so many young blokes that look up to us’ Pauline Hanson’s claims that the national men’s football team represented a monocultural Australia angered many Socceroos during this year’s World Cup, Nestory Irankunda has said. The One Nation leader’s comments came a week after the team beat Turkey in their opening match of the group stage at the tournament in North America. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Players upset ‘because there’s so many young blokes that look up to us’

Pauline Hanson’s claims that the national men’s football team represented a monocultural Australia angered many Socceroos during this year’s World Cup, Nestory Irankunda has said.

The One Nation leader’s comments came a week after the team beat Turkey in their opening match of the group stage at the tournament in North America.

After her National Press Club speech , in which she declared Australia cannot be multicultural and must exist as a “monocultural society”, Hanson hit back at claims the team would not have won the game under her policy. She said: “The Socceroos represent my vision of a monocultural Australia.”

But Irankunda, the forward who scored Australia’s first goal of the tournament during the match in Vancouver, said many Socceroos disagreed with her comments.

“It did make a lot of us boys angry – I won’t lie,” he ABC radio on Wednesday. “I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it.

“I always tell people I’m Australian, and it really did upset me, and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that, especially because there’s so many young blokes that look up to us.”

The 20-year-old, who moved to Portuguese champions Sporting CP for a reported fee of up to $32m following his World Cup success, was born in a Tanzanian refugee camp to Burundian parents.

Fellow Socceroo Awer Mabil was born in a Kenyan refugee camp to South Sudanese parents and was named Young Australian of the Year in 2023.

After the team was knocked out of the World Cup, Mabil hit back at Hanson’s suggestion Australia was not a multicultural society, calling her claims “bullshit” .

Earlier in the tournament, Australian players released a video embracing the team’s migrant roots, in which midfielder Jackson Irvine said: “The Socceroos aren’t just a team, we are a reflection of modern Australia.”

“There’s people like me and Awer, Mohamed Touré that go out there … and try to do the right thing, and we do, do the right thing,” Irankunda said.

“I don’t like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people that do bad.”

Asked if he would speak with the One Nation senator, the 20-year-old poured cold water on the suggestion.

“I’m still upset about some of the things she said in the past,” he said. “I’m not someone who likes to jump into controversial things or political stuff, but you never know – one day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting.”

articles.title: ‘Why do you never buy a round?!’ 20 mortifying money conversations with friends – and how to handle them
articles.summary: Whether it’s paying for dinner, going on holiday or sharing a taxi, friendships can be fraught with financial frustrations, which are very rarely aired. Here’s how to break the taboo Summer is the season of socialising, from alfresco drinks to weddings to group holidays. It can get expensive – and suddenly you start noticing those friends who don’t pay their way. Or the ones who splash the cash and make you feel cheap. In fact, there are a host of annoying money-related habits that can cause tension among friends. Here are 20 common sources of financial frustration – and how to resolve them. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Whether it’s paying for dinner, going on holiday or sharing a taxi, friendships can be fraught with financial frustrations, which are very rarely aired. Here’s how to break the taboo

S ummer is the season of socialising, from alfresco drinks to weddings to group holidays. It can get expensive – and suddenly you start noticing those friends who don’t pay their way. Or the ones who splash the cash and make you feel cheap. In fact, there are a host of annoying money-related habits that can cause tension among friends. Here are 20 common sources of financial frustration – and how to resolve them.

British pub etiquette seems simple: in a group of friends, everyone takes it in turns to buy the drinks. In practice, it is a minefield. There’s always someone who hangs back in the hope it won’t come round to them; someone who orders half a lager when it’s their turn to pay and a double G&T when it’s yours; couples who see themselves as one entity when it comes to paying, but not when it comes to drinking.

Ellie Austin-Williams , the London-based author of Money Talks: A Lifestyle Guide for Financial Wellbeing , says it is best to bring it up straight away. “Have the conversation at the start: do you want to do a round, or shall we pay our own way?” Isn’t that a bit embarrassing? “People feel it’s too awkward, but it’s better to say: ‘I’ll buy my own, I’m not drinking today.’ People really do respect that.” Conversely, if you’ve all agreed upfront to do rounds, it’s harder for someone to shirk their turn.

Matt Altmix, who is based in Atlanta, Georgia, and co-hosts the podcast How to Money , suggests budgeting for pub trips. If you’re happy with how much you’ve decided to spend that night, you don’t need to obsess about what everyone else is doing. “That way, you’re actually having a good time,” says Altmix. Warning: this may mean going to the pub less often. “Skipping out sometimes is totally acceptable,” he says. “Then when you do show up, make it count.”

Alex Holder , who lives in Lewes, East Sussex, is the author of Open Up: Why Talking About Money Will Change Your Life . She rejects round culture altogether. “It’s presuming we’re all going to drink the same amount. Not everyone wants to drink five drinks,” she says. “Rather than noticing that someone gets a cheap drink when they’re paying and feeling enraged, exit the culture.”

Going out for dinner with friends is fraught with financial pitfalls. Do you simply divide the bill by the number of people? That’s a rough deal for the teetotal vegetarian with a small appetite, who ends up subsidising someone else’s steak, sides and wine. Do you pay only for what you ordered? That can seem petty – and somehow there’s always a shortfall.

Joel Larsgaard, Altmix’s best friend and co-host, says: “Typically, the things that add up are the drinks, the appetisers and the dessert. You can still go out and enjoy a nice dinner without overspending if you avoid those big culprits. But you don’t get the savings in the same way if you split a bill with somebody and they’re like: ‘Yeah, I got three cocktails and the fancy tiramisu.’”

Altmix suggests bringing it up in a lighthearted way: “‘Man, Sam’s over there just throwing down the steak, am I right?!’ There’s a way you can have those conversations without it feeling judgmental. Crack some jokes, be light about it and hopefully it leads to some healthy conversation.”

Of course, this approach won’t go down well with everyone. “To some, it’s normal to split the bill,” says Holder. “Not to is an attack on what they ordered.”

Austin-Williams would rather discuss money matters before dinner: “Try to bring it into the conversation when you’re planning. If friends want to go to a fancy restaurant, say: ‘Can we just get a burger? I’m on a budget.’”

Alternatively, raise it before ordering, she says. For example: “‘I’ve got a maximum of £30, so I’m just going to have a main, but you have what you want.’” Failing that, speak up when the bill arrives. You could say: “‘I didn’t have as much and I’m trying to watch my spending this month – is it OK if we pay per item this time?’” She says people worry about looking cheap and not being part of the group, but often others will be relieved that someone has spoken up.

“I believe we should tip because, unfortunately, that is the way that hospitality staff are paid properly. It’s a really hard job with low wages,” says Holder. She understands why some people may dislike the tipping system: “These things feel emotionally fraught: you feel deceived, that the establishment is out to get you.” However, like everyone else I speak to, she feels tipping is non-negotiable.

Larsgaard advises factoring in the tip when budgeting to eat out. “You cannot let your financial situation dictate how much you tip. If you can’t afford it, that is just a sign that you should be eating at home,” he says. “If you don’t want to tip, that’s not frugal, it’s cheap. That’s how we make a distinction: you’re being cheap when your attempts to save money are coming at someone else’s expense.”

Austin-Williams prefers to take charge, saying something like: “‘Can everyone add £2 for the tip?’” But Holder says: “You can’t make friends tip; everyone has different money rules. Work out your own relationship with tipping.”

If Larsgaard were to notice a friend hadn’t tipped, “that would probably make me mad enough to either leave more on my tip or have a conversation. ‘Did you see how hard she was working? Do you know how much she gets paid?’ I think sometimes people don’t understand the economics of being a server.”

Some people insist on being in the front row; others are happiest in the cheap seats. Often, these preferences have no correlation to bank balances. “Some things can be triggers for certain people, such as spending on theatre tickets or taxis,” says Holder. “Others find it easier to spend on experiences than things.” So what do you do if you’re misaligned with a friend?

Austin-Williams would try to compromise with a high spender. “Say: ‘I’d really like to go, but £70 seats are a bit out of budget at the moment. If you really want to go front row, count me out this time. If not, £30 tickets are fine,’” she says. “Give them the option – they’d probably rather go with you.” You can do similar with a low spender, saying, for example, that you struggled to see from the £10 seats last time, so would prefer to spend a little more if possible.

Larsgaard has other ways to compromise. “Maybe you take one for the team. You’re front row at this one because you both love this artist, then you either skip the next concert or sit in the cheap seats at that one. Or hang out before the show, go together, but sit in different spots.”

No one likes to be a letdown, but sometimes you have to decline an invitation. “One of my friends was just in Europe and went to see Harry Styles at Wembley,” says Larsgaard. “I was like: ‘No, sorry, I can’t afford that right now. Let’s put the record on at my house. If you can afford it, man, go and have an awesome time. I will be a little bit jealous, but also psyched for you.’”

“If you are a type A person who likes to plan everything,” this can happen, says Altmix. Friends may have every intention of getting the tickets next time, but just don’t get the chance. “If you kick back a little bit, that gives them an opportunity to, right? People work at different speeds and have different things going on in their lives and maybe they’re just in a really busy season.”

Austin-Williams says: “If you’re noticing a bit of a pattern, stop offering. Next time, say: ‘I’ll get mine,’ or: ‘Let’s just get our own.’ If your friendship is in danger, raise it: ‘I picked up the bill the last couple of times, would you mind getting it this time?’ Often, people just haven’t been paying attention.”

“Don’t presume that everyone has a collective relationship with money,” says Holder. “Some people find paying money back really difficult; they almost have a block.” She says most people will appreciate it if you are “very straight up” and text with your bank details.

If that doesn’t work, you’ll have to talk to them. “Have a really frank conversation,” says Austin-Williams. “Things happen – your car breaks down, you lose your job. It’s important to understand if your friend is struggling.”

Express concern, rather than making accusations, says Larsgaard. “‘Hey, I noticed you said you were going to pay and you didn’t. Is everything OK?’” They may simply apologise for forgetting, or they may open up about money worries. “It’s very easy to be a jerk, but they’re your friend. Asking a question about what’s going on gives you a chance for deeper connection and understanding.”

When you’re popping to the shops, some friends think nothing of placing an order, even if you haven’t offered. It might only be a couple of quid here and there, but even low-level freeloading can be annoying over time. What should you do?

“You’re thinking: I would never do that,” says Holder. But everyone is different: it has probably never crossed your friend’s mind that you might begrudge them a Diet Coke. “You can a) have a conversation, b) continue to be bothered or c) get over it,” she says. Unless money is really tight, getting over it seems the best option here.

It may feel as though you’re always the one paying for the taxi or doing the driving and that your friends are taking advantage. It’s probably not that calculated, says Holder. “Someone might think: ‘You’re always getting an Uber; I’ll get in it as I’m going that way.’ Accept that their norm about money may not be yours,” she says. “Rather than getting mad with friends, take responsibility for your own spending. For example, if you often give a friend a lift, either ask them for petrol money or don’t agree to drive them places.”

What if they said they’d contribute, but haven’t? “Always assume it’s unintentional,” says Austin-Williams. “Give them a nudge: ‘Just doing my budget and wondered if you could send that Uber fare over?’ Most friends just need that nudge.”

Ideally, says Holder, “holiday with people who are willing to spend a similar amount to you. Don’t holiday with really rich people or accept it’s really going to bug you!”

Altmix will only travel with someone he knows well. “You’ve got to pay for everything when you’re travelling, right? Everything costs money. You wake up, you’re paying for something: you’ve got to get some coffee, you’ve got to get some breakfast. There are all these money decisions throughout the day. And if you haven’t established an understanding of how much you like to spend and the type of travelling that you like to do, I think you could be in a world of hurt financially and from a relational standpoint.”

Be clear about your expectations at the planning stage, says Austin-Williams. “Be specific. ‘This is my budget for the whole trip; this is my budget for the accommodation. Who’s going to pay? What’s the repayment schedule?’ There’s a chance you won’t be able to align.”

Larsgaard says: “It comes down to honesty and having those conversations up front. ‘Yeah, I’d like to go to Spain, but how do you feel about a hotel versus a B&B? Likewise, a family with children will pay more for a bigger room with extras such as additional beds or an en suite.”

Too complicated? Holder says this is one of the few occasions when she would recommend using AI: “You can outline the scenario and it will do the maths for you.” Failing that, “organise separate accommodation near each other”.

You budgeted for the travel and accommodation and thought you had plenty for food and activities, but now your friends want to eat at fancy restaurants and go on expensive excursions. Do you have to miss out?

Groups have different ways of sharing holiday costs: some take it in turns to pay, some pay into a kitty, others keep a spreadsheet or use apps such as Splitwise . “There is no single ‘best’ way to share costs on holiday,” says Green. “The key thing is to be honest about how you’d prefer to do it before the holiday starts. Nor is she a huge fan of technological solutions. “Apps can help, but some people forget to add their costs, while some people add every little thing,” she says. “It’s better if everyone has a night when they’re catering.”

Austin-Williams thinks these send-offs “have got a bit out of hand” and are one of the most difficult situations to handle with friends. “If you don’t want to go to an expensive hen do abroad, honesty is the best policy,” she says. “A really good friend doesn’t want you to rack up debts. However, “if it’s a really close friend, you find ways to afford it”, says Altmix. “That doesn’t mean putting it on a credit card. British pub etiquette seems simple: in a group of friends, everyone takes it in turns to buy the drinks. In practice, it is a minefield. There’s always someone who hangs back in the hope it won’t come round to them; someone who orders half a lager when it’s their turn to pay and a double G&T when it’s yours; couples who see themselves as one entity when it comes to paying, but not when it comes to drinking.

Ellie Austin-Williams , the London-based author of Money Talks: A Lifestyle Guide for Financial Wellbeing , says it is best to bring it up straight away. “Have the conversation at the start: do you want to do a round, or shall we pay our own way?” Isn’t that a bit embarrassing? “People feel it’s too awkward, but it’s better to say: ‘I’ll buy my own, I’m not drinking today.’ People really do respect that.” Conversely, if you’ve all agreed upfront to do rounds, it’s harder for someone to shirk their turn.

Matt Altmix, who is based in Atlanta, Georgia, and co-hosts the podcast How to Money , suggests budgeting for pub trips. If you’re happy with how much you’ve decided to spend that night, you don’t need to obsess about what everyone else is doing. “That way, you’re actually having a good time,” says Altmix. She rejects round culture altogether. “It’s presuming we’re all going to drink the same amount. Not everyone wants to drink five drinks,” she says. “Rather than noticing that someone gets a cheap drink when they’re paying and feeling enraged, exit the culture.”

Going out for dinner with friends is fraught with financial pitfalls. Do you simply divide the bill by the number of people? “I believe we should tip because, unfortunately, that is the way that hospitality staff are paid properly. It’s a really hard job with low wages,” says Holder. articles.title: Brewers shell Mariners 22-0, tied for largest shutout win in 139 years
articles.summary: Milwaukee match major-league record dating to 1887 Yelich, Hamilton and Lara hit three-run home runs Catcher Sánchez completes five-hitter with slowballs The Milwaukee Brewers matched baseball’s modern-era record for the biggest shutout, beating the Seattle Mariners 22-0 on Tuesday night behind three-run homers from Christian Yelich, David Hamilton and Luis Lara and a two-run shot by Jake Bauers. The major league-best Brewers (78-48) matched a franchise record for runs in a game. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers matched baseball’s modern-era record for the biggest shutout, beating the Seattle Mariners 22-0 on Tuesday night behind three-run homers from Christian Yelich, David Hamilton and Luis Lara and a two-run shot by Jake Bauers.

The major league-best Brewers (78-48) matched a franchise record for runs in a game.

It equalled the most lopsided shutout win in Major League Baseball since 28 June 1887, when the Philadelphia Phillies won 24-0 at the Indianapolis Hoosiers.

In the modern era (since 1901), the only previous 22-0 victories were by Pittsburgh over the host Chicago Cubs on 16 September 1975 and by Cleveland at the New York Yankees on 31 August 2004.

Bauers scored the Brewers’ first run in colorful fashion. He doubled with two outs in the first against Bryce Miller (4-7). William Contreras singled, and left fielder Randy Arozarena’s throw to the plate easily beat Bauers, who slapped at catcher Cal Raleigh’s mitt on his slide. Raleigh dropped the ball, and Bauers dived back to the plate.

Yelich’s homer made it 6-0 in the fifth. Hamilton went deep in the sixth to make it 9-0, and Bauers’ 22nd homer later in the inning made it 11-0.

Milwaukee scored nine times in the eighth against Mariners infielder Leo Rivas, including Lara’s homer, which was the first of his career.

Kyle Harrison (10-3), who allowed eight runs (three earned) over 4 2/3 innings in his previous start, held the Mariners to two hits in five innings. Shane Drohan worked two innings, Grant Anderson pitched the eighth and catcher Gary Sánchez completed the five-hitter, working around two hits in the ninth while throwing several pitches under 40 mph.

Hamilton’s four RBIs were a career high. Yelich and Lara also drove in four runs each, and Garrett Mitchell had four hits.

articles.title: Multiple brawls overshadow Saints-Cowboys joint practice session
articles.summary: Saints’ Bell alert as he was driven from the field At least six fights mar joint practice at training camp Donovan Ezeiruaku ejected for throwing punches New Orleans wide receiver Ronnie Bell was carted off the field because of the effects of Southern California heat after being involved in one of several fights during a chippy joint practice between the Saints and Dallas Cowboys on Tuesday. “He just had to go inside for a little bit. He just got a little bit overheated,” New Orleans coach Kellen Moore said. Continue reading...
articles.content:
New Orleans wide receiver Ronnie Bell was carted off the field because of the effects of Southern California heat after being involved in one of several fights during a chippy joint practice between the Saints and Dallas Cowboys on Tuesday.

“He just had to go inside for a little bit. He just got a little bit overheated,” New Orleans coach Kellen Moore said.

Bell walked to the trainer’s tent following a second brawl between the Saints offense and Cowboys defense. Several minutes later, he was put onto a cart with his jersey and shoulder pads off. Bell was alert and sitting up as he was driven off the field.

Bell is going into his fourth season in the NFL out of Michigan. He has 10 receptions for 113 yards and four touchdowns in 28 games with the San Francisco 49ers and Saints.

Temperatures were in the high 70s Fahrenheit (around 25C) and it felt hotter because of unusually high humidity for the region caused by El Nino, seemingly exacerbating the intensity of a two-hour workout that nearly devolved into chaos on multiple occasions.

The early fracases happened on the field closest to fans where the Cowboys offense and Saints defense were scrimmaging.

Tensions carried over to the far field, where Dallas outside linebacker Donovan Ezeiruaku got into a confrontation with several New Orleans players before teammates surrounded them in a massive scrum, with Saints center Erik McCoy throwing a Cowboys helmet high into the air.

Ezeiruaku and McCoy later came to blows , leading to the second-year defender from Boston College being ejected for throwing punches. It was the second time in training camp that Ezeiruaku has been booted for fisticuffs. He was ejected from a Week 18 loss to the New York Giants for pulling a helmet off an offensive lineman.

“We’ll have a long conversation, you know,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said. “Donovan’s a very bright young man, and, again, he understands he can’t hurt the football team. It’s part of a growth mindset for him.”

At the same time, Schottenheimer indicated an appreciation for players being willing to stand up for themselves and their teammates.

“To be very, very clear, we’re not taking (expletive) from anybody, but we also have to have the discipline to not play over the edge and hurt the football team, get penalties, do things like that,” he said.

In spite of those outbursts, Moore was largely pleased with the work the Saints did in the first of two joint practices this week. They will work with the Los Angeles Rams on Thursday.

“Not the ideal flow of the joint practice, but we got the work that we needed,” Moore said.

“Honestly, I got to go look at the film ’cause I was playing referee the whole time,” Schottenheimer said. “Our football team needs this work, and overall, I was disappointed in the work today because I didn’t think we got enough good work. I thought there were too many bodies on the ground, and it just felt sloppy to me.”

The Cowboys offense and Saints defense both came onto the field wearing white jerseys because of a miscommunication, prompting New Orleans staffers to scramble to find contrasting black tops.

“My last name is Tyree today, and you could mistake me for a receiver,” linebacker Pete Werner joked, wearing a slim-cut No. 89 jersey instead of his usual No. 20. “I actually like the number, it’s a little small, it’s kind of snug, so it felt pretty good. I felt fast.”

Saints running back Alvin Kamara left practice early because of a knee injury, and cornerback Quincy Riley departed with a groin injury. Moore did not immediately know the severity of those injuries.

articles.title: Sydney Swans ‘embarrassed and ashamed’ as five players stood down for breach of standards
articles.summary: Bice, Blakey, Heeney, Jordon and Warner hit by suspensions None of the five players have been arrested or charged The Sydney Swans CEO says the club is “deeply embarrassed and ashamed” for its players’ apparent failure to maintain the club’s standards at a hotel during the early hours of Monday, suspending them for the remainder of the season. The club stood down players Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner on Wednesday morning. None of the men have been arrested or charged, but have been connected to the police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Sydney Swans CEO says the club is “deeply embarrassed and ashamed” for its players’ apparent failure to maintain the club’s standards at a hotel during the early hours of Monday, suspending them for the remainder of the season.

The club stood down players Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner on Wednesday morning. None of the men have been arrested or charged, but have been connected to the police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Chief executive Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Wednesday afternoon alongside chair Andrew Pridham.

“To say we’re disappointed is an understatement,” Pavlich said. “We’re deeply embarrassed and ashamed [of] the poor choices of five of our players, and the impact that’s had on the women involved, and also the club, our supporters, and so many other people.”

“We respect that this is an ongoing investigation by Victoria police, and the actions we’ve taken today are totally independent of this,” Pavlich said.

The former Fremantle player, who took the Swans top job last year, said the players’ behaviour fell short of the club’s standards.

“It was staying out late, it was drinking, it was continuing their night, it was bringing women back to the hotel, it was a long way short of what we expect from our players and we’re holding them to a really high standard, but they were well short of anything near that standard,” he said.

Pavlich said coaching staff including head coach Dean Cox, who were pictured out late on the same evening, had not breached any standards, and the possible introduction of a curfew would be a decision for Cox, his staff and players.

Pridham said both his chief executive and head coach retained his confidence. “[These are] the actions, very unfortunate actions, of five players in relation to breaching our standards, and that really relates to them. I think to extrapolate beyond that, I think is very unfair.”

Pavlich said this instance did not reflect the club’s culture and its attitude towards women. “All I’ve seen so far at this football club, barring this significant incident, is that we are one club and we treat and respect women incredibly well, and it’s of the utmost importance to our football club.”

Pridham issued a broad apology to the community, the fans and corporate partners, and pledged to work to restore people’s trust in the club.

“Our thoughts go out to everybody who’s been impacted by these events, and we know it’s impacted many, many people ranging from the partners of our staff, our players, our women’s programme, our men’s programme.”

Pavlich did not address any alleged victims in his initial address on Wednesday, but was asked about them by reporters on Wednesday. “We’re deeply concerned about their welfare and the wellbeing of those women, and we offer as much support as we can,” he said, while recognising it would be inappropriate to contact them while there is a police investigation ongoing.

“They’re the ones who are impacted severely at the moment, and we are here to acknowledge those allegations.”

Pridham said the sanctions have all but ended the Swans’ hopes of winning a first premiership since 2012. “To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this just tells you how seriously we’re taking it.”

Yet Pavlich said he would not write off Sydney’s AFL season. “I am always optimistic of what our club, what our people can do,” he said.

The Swans are hosting their first double header this Sunday, with both AFL and AFLW games to be held at the SCG. “It’s going to be difficult,” Pridham said.

“But our approach very much will be to celebrate having a historic double header with the women’s team playing, and I know they’re very excited about that.

“And we just have to make it as normal as possible and clearly respecting the circumstances of this week is going to make that difficult, but we’re hopeful that our fans turn up and, to the extent they feel willing to do so, come and support the teams.”

articles.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 15: Manchester City
articles.summary: With the departures of Pep Guardiola and Rodri it looks like the end of an era at City. Will Enzo Maresca be able to sustain their position as a domestic and continental superpower? Guardian writers’ predicted position: 2nd (NB: this is not necessarily Jamie Jackson’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips) Last season’s position: 2nd Continue reading...
articles.content:
With the departures of Pep Guardiola and Rodri it looks like the end of an era at City. Will Enzo Maresca be able to sustain their position as a domestic and continental superpower?

Guardian writers’ predicted position: 2nd (NB: this is not necessarily Jamie Jackson’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Enzo Maresca was already in herculean task mode by signing on as the man charged with continuing the dynasty built by Pep Guardiola at Manchester City before Rodri decided to leave the club and join Barcelona. The 30-year-old may be headed for a second Ballon d’Or after his displays in Spain’s triumphant World Cup campaign, so the loss of a midfielder capable of moulding games domestically and in the Champions League represents a sizeable blow for Maresca.

There are further negatives too, with John Stones, Nathan Aké and Bernardo Silva also no longer at City. On the positive side, Elliot Anderson has joined for £116m from Nottingham Forest having impressed for England at the World Cup. City’s new manager also has Erling Haaland, who will be favourite to claim a fourth Premier League Golden Boot in five seasons. Less certain is how Phil Foden will perform despite being boosted by a bumper new contract. Can the boy from Stockport dovetail with Rayan Cherki and once more pull the strings for his boyhood side?

City are a best-in-class organisation, who can be used as an exemplar of how to pursue excellence on and off the field. This, of course, would change were they found guilty over the 130 charges brought against them for alleged breaches of Premier League rules. It has been more than three years since the charges were announced, with City continuing to deny any wrongdoing. The new Pep Guardiola Stand, opened for the great man’s final home game last season, means 61,000 fans can now witness Haaland and co go to work, the Etihad Stadium’s capacity having previously stood at 53,400.

Sheikh Mansour is a hero to the City faithful for a glittering period of ownership that has elevated their team to a domestic and continental superpower. Listening to fans, the club have also frozen ticket prices for a third consecutive season. Meanwhile in the Pep Guardiola Stand, 4,000 new flexi season tickets – a pay-as-you-go scheme – have sold out, half of which are for junior fans, with City introducing £10 seats for those who live in the five wards around the ground.

Is Maresca courageous for following The Man or naive for believing he can? Over to the 46-year-old, who has zero doubt the City job is no chalice laced with poison. “It’s fantastic, nice and exciting, and for me, a privilege,” he said. “First of all, the most important thing has been that Khaldoon [al-Mubarak, the chair], Hugo [Viana, the director of football] and Ferran [Soriano, the chief executive] all speak the same language in terms of this is a club that has to win games, titles and has to compete, but we also talk about how we can continue to make this club better, season after season.” Maresca’s CV shows the Championship crown with Leicester, and the Conference League and Club World Cup glory with Chelsea. How he would love to add the Premier League title to that roll of honour at the first time of asking.

Rodri’s departure offers Anderson an opportunity to run City’s midfield. Can he do so? Maresca and Viana obviously believe this or £116m would not have been splurged on the lad from Whitley Bay who could not nail down a starting berth for Newcastle in five years as a senior professional there. At the World Cup there were flashes of a schemer who can spray passes long range – Rodri-style – as well as the shorter, metronomic stuff. What’s for sure is that Anderson has a career-defining opportunity in front of him.

Manchester City conceded more league goals from set pieces last season than they had in the previous two campaigns combined. They were costly at times too: the winning goals in their losses at Aston Villa and Newcastle both came from corners, for instance. Maresca’s Chelsea conceded from a set play every three league games so his record there was a shade worse than City’s in 2025-26. He has work to do.

Vitor Reis was signed in January 2025 and made four appearances that season. The defender’s debut was also forgettable as, then 19, he was hooked at half-time with City trailing 1-0 at Leyton Orient in the FA Cup fourth round. The Brazilian played all of the 3-1 victory in the following round, and was fielded in the 89th-minute of the 2-0 league victory at Leicester in April before his sole other City appearance: a full outing in the 2-0 Club World Cup win over Wydad Casablanca that June. Last season’s loan at City’s sister club Girona ended in relegation, but Reis is said to have impressed.

The departed Rodri made real the ultimate fantasy of all players by captaining his country to the World Cup and being so vital to that glory that he was named player of the tournament. Cherki fared less well, making six substitute appearances and one start for a France side that fell, to Spain, in the semi-finals . France’s attacking ranks may overflow with quality, but for a player with magic in both boots, that seemed odd.

Over to the 46-year-old, who has zero doubt the City job is no chalice laced with poison. “It’s fantastic, nice and exciting, and for me, a privilege,” he said. “First of all, the most important thing has been that Khaldoon [al-Mubarak, the chair], Hugo [Viana, the director of football] and Ferran [Soriano, the chief executive] all speak the same language in terms of this is a club that has to win games, titles and has to compete, but we also talk about how we can continue to make this club better, season after season.” Maresca’s CV shows the Championship crown with Leicester, and the Conference League and Club World Cup glory with Chelsea. How he would love to add the Premier League title to that roll of honour at the first time of asking.

Rodri’s departure offers Anderson an opportunity to run City’s midfield. Can he do so? Maresca and Viana obviously believe this or £116m would not have been splurged on the lad from Whitley Bay who could not nail down a starting berth for Newcastle in five years as a senior professional there. At the World Cup there were flashes of a schemer who can spray passes long range – Rodri-style – as well as the shorter, metronomic stuff. What’s for sure is that Anderson has a career-defining opportunity in front of him.

Manchester City conceded more league goals from set pieces last season than they had in the previous two campaigns combined. They were costly at times too: the winning goals in their losses at Aston Villa and Newcastle both came from corners, for instance. Maresca’s Chelsea conceded from a set play every three league games so his record there was a shade worse than City’s in 2025-26. He has work to do.

Vitor Reis was signed in January 2025 and made four appearances that season. The defender’s debut was also forgettable as, then 19, he was hooked at half-time with City trailing 1-0 at Leyton Orient in the FA Cup fourth round. The Brazilian played all of the 3-1 victory in the following round, and was fielded in the 89th-minute of the 2-0 league victory at Leicester in April before his sole other City appearance: a full outing in the 2-0 Club World Cup win over Wydad Casablanca that June. Last season’s loan at City’s sister club Girona ended in relegation, but Reis is said to have impressed.

The departed Rodri made real the ultimate fantasy of all players by captaining his country to the World Cup and being so vital to that glory that he was named player of the tournament. Cherki fared less well, making six substitute appearances and one start for a France side that fell, to Spain, in the semi-finals . France’s attacking ranks may overflow with quality, but for a player with magic in both boots, that seemed odd.

articles.title: In Zavier Gozo, Crystal Palace land a US prospect living up to the hype
articles.summary: The 19-year-old US youth international has turned heads in MLS this year, and is on the cusp of a USMNT breakthrough For much of the past year, the story of American starlet Zavier Gozo has been one of realizing potential – even in failure. Speaking with the Guardian the day after he and Real Salt Lake teammate Diego Luna learned they wouldn’t be on Mauricio Pochettino’s squad for this summer’s World Cup, the 19-year-old Gozo admitted the rejection made him realize how close he’d gotten to earning a spot. “I thought I would be less disappointed than I was,” Gozo said in May . “Obviously, it wasn’t like I was supposed to go. I feel like I was disappointed, but I also think it just gave me so much more motivation to be able to make the first team, whenever that is.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
The 19-year-old US youth international has turned heads in MLS this year, and is on the cusp of a USMNT breakthrough

F or much of the past year, the story of American starlet Zavier Gozo has been one of realizing potential – even in failure. Speaking with the Guardian the day after he and Real Salt Lake teammate Diego Luna learned they wouldn’t be on Mauricio Pochettino’s squad for this summer’s World Cup, the 19-year-old Gozo admitted the rejection made him realize how close he’d gotten to earning a spot.

“I thought I would be less disappointed than I was,” Gozo said in May . “Obviously, it wasn’t like I was supposed to go. I feel like I was disappointed, but I also think it just gave me so much more motivation to be able to make the first team, whenever that is.”

If it works out well, Gozo’s move to Crystal Palace could see that happen sooner than many would have anticipated a year ago. The Premier League club finalized the transfer of Gozo from Real Salt Lake on Tuesday in a five-year deal. The agreement is reportedly worth around $15m (£11m).

The move follows one of the most rapid ascents of any American men’s prospect in recent memory.

Gozo joined the Real Salt Lake academy in 2021 at age 14, debuting with their second team, Real Monarchs, a year later. His MLS debut came in 2023, when he was still just 16. Over time, Gozo emerged as an option at right wing-back offering precocious confidence on the ball, capping his first full season with RSL with four goals and three assists in 1,810 minutes.

This season, Gozo has been given increased license to stay upfield. His technique in close quarters has been especially impressive, with deft touches and passes helping RSL get into dangerous areas. His end product has also been on greater display, with six goals and five assists in 1,417 minutes thus far.

His ability to set up his own shot as well as create dangerous looks for his teammates helps him stand out. Gozo has made 67 progressive carries upfield, per Futi, a category led by Lionel Messi, Denis Bouanga, Evander and Anders Dreyer – four members of last year’s MLS Best XI.

The question for any young player of Gozo’s caliber is how best to position themselves for international consideration. On the one hand, he had already established himself as a regular starter in MLS. On the other, strong performances in MLS – as in any league – provide no guarantee of landing on a national team, as Gozo’s teammate Luna learned the hard way by being among Pochettino’s toughest omissions.

As a result, Gozo felt he was nearing the ideal window for making a move across the Atlantic.

“I feel like I’m ready to go,” Gozo added without hesitation. “Whether that happens or not, I don’t know, but I think this is a unique situation I have. I’m blessed to be in a situation where I have such a good club to be at, but I also think, you know … What’s next in my career? I don’t know.”

The son of an American mother and an Ivorian father, Gozo also earned his first US youth international callup in 2022, beginning with the U-15s. He has become a regular with the youth national teams.

With Pochettino opting to stick with the USMNT through the 2030 World Cup, Gozo figures to be in contention with the players who made the squad for this summer’s tournament for a place in the US’s plans over the next four years. Training at Palace every day with US mainstay Chris Richards will surely keep him in Pochettino’s sights, to say nothing of any Premier League minutes he’s able to get under new manager Pierre Sage.

articles.title: Jamal Musiala says ‘treatable seizures’ are reason for two collapses in four days
articles.summary: Musiala reveals ‘neurological dysfunction’ diagnosis Winger has fallen to floor during two recent friendlies The Bayern Munich winger Jamal Musiala has revealed he is suffering from “treatable absence seizures” after he collapsed on the pitch for the second time in four days. Musiala fell to the floor eight minutes after coming on as a substitute in Bayern’s friendly with Heidenheim on Tuesday night. The 23-year-old experienced a similar incident during Saturday’s friendly against RB Leipzig, but Musiala has insisted there is no long-term health risk. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Bayern Munich winger Jamal Musiala has revealed he is suffering from “treatable absence seizures” after he collapsed on the pitch for the second time in four days.

Musiala fell to the floor eight minutes after coming on as a substitute in Bayern’s friendly with Heidenheim on Tuesday night. The 23-year-old experienced a similar incident during Saturday’s friendly against RB Leipzig, but Musiala has insisted there is no long-term health risk.

“First things first, I am doing well. I am incredibly grateful for your messages and your support!” Musiala posted on Instagram . “I understand that many of you are worried. I would like to put those concerns to rest today and explain the situation.

“I have been diagnosed with brief, temporary – but treatable – absence seizures resulting from a neurological dysfunction. These can lead to the kind of incidents seen recently, such as during the match against Leipzig or the game in Heidenheim.

“I know they might look alarming at first glance, but for me, they are currently part of my everyday life. I am receiving excellent medical care and remain very optimistic. FC Bayern and my personal support network are right by my side, helping me through this. Importantly, there is no further health risk involved.”

The Germany international added: “In close consultation and regular contact with the experts, it was my personal wish to face this challenge; with the medical clearance of the neurologists, I want to continue doing what helps my recovery most: simply living my life and pursuing my passion for playing football.”

Having come on for Ismael Saibari after 61 minutes against Heidenheim, Musiala was replaced by Cassiano Kiala eight minutes later. He appeared dazed as he received medical treatment and was helped off the pitch, with Bayern’s sporting director, Max Eberl, moving to play down concerns soon after the game.

“Jamal will speak about this in the near future. We knew about it and we are aware of the situation,” Eberl said.

Bayern won the game 4-2, with Felipe Chávez, Arijon Ibrahimovic, Luis Díaz and Nathaniel Brown all on target. Musiala also required medical attention after collapsing in the match against RB Leipzig.

articles.title: Wladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’
articles.summary: Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’ Hayden Panettiere ’s daughter will be raised to remember her mother’s “immense talent” and “incredible career”, according to a tribute posted on social media on Tuesday by Wladimir Klitschko, the ex-lineal world heavyweight boxing champion and the late Hollywood actor’s former partner. Their daughter, Kaya, has been raised by the Ukrainian retired boxer since 2018, when Panettiere ceded full custody to concentrate on her battles with alcoholism, depression and substance abuse. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Boxing champion says he will raise their daughter, Kaya, to remember the late actor’s ‘immense talent’

Hayden Panettiere ’s daughter will be raised to remember her mother’s “immense talent” and “incredible career”, according to a tribute posted on social media on Tuesday by Wladimir Klitschko, the ex-lineal world heavyweight boxing champion and the late Hollywood actor’s former partner.

Their daughter, Kaya, has been raised by the Ukrainian retired boxer since 2018, when Panettiere ceded full custody to concentrate on her battles with alcoholism, depression and substance abuse.

Her death in Greenville, South Carolina, was reported on Sunday , with no cause given.

“Our family is going through a time of profound shock and grief,” Klitschko wrote in the Instagram post, which featured a photograph of himself and Panettiere smiling at a beach, with Kaya – whose face is obscured – perched on her mother’s shoulders.

“The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon. Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.”

The message also referenced the troubles that the Nashville and Heroes actor had experienced at a young age, following a succession of child stars who faced later challenges or tragedy .

“She built an incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry,” Klitschko wrote of Panettiere. “Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives.

“To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was.”

Klitschko also sent his condolences to Panettiere’s grieving parents, friends and fans.

“Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon,” boxing’s lineal heavyweight champion from 2009 to 2015 wrote. “I ask everyone to please respect our family’s feelings and privacy during this incredibly difficult time. For now, this is all I wish to say.

In May, Panettiere expressed hope that she would one day be reunited with her daughter, who was born in 2014.

“I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she told podcaster Jay Shetty in an emotional interview.

“I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.”

Klitschko and Panettiere met at a book launch party in 2009, when the actor, then aged 20, was already a television star for her appearances as fictional high school cheerleader Claire Bennet in Heroes. After first splitting in 2011, they remained close friends and became engaged in 2013. Panettiere gave birth to Kaya a year later.

The actor struggled with postpartum depression, and the couple split for good in 2018, with Kaya spending time with her father at residences in Florida and Europe, E! News reported at the time.

Panettiere then had an on-again, off-again relationship with Brian Hickerson. The Associated Press and NBC News on Tuesday reported they had obtained a police report that said Hickerson and his brother, Zach, were at the scene inside the apartment complex where Panettiere died.

The report said Hickerson showed police “a bag of medication” that Panettiere was taking at the time of her death, according to NBC.

Panettiere’s relationship with Hickerson was marred by domestic abuse allegations. He was arrested multiple times and reportedly jailed in 2021 after pleading no contest to domestic abuse charges.

articles.title: Social media on trial as $200bn case against Facebook and Instagram begins
articles.summary: Twenty-nine US states are seeking huge damages, claiming Meta’s platforms were addictive by design In 1994, more than 40 US states came together to sue one of the most powerful industries on Earth: big tobacco. The suits brought together diverse claims centred on tobacco companies’ misleading advertising and contribution to a mounting public health crisis. They ended in a negotiated settlement with the US government, in which the companies agreed to pay more than any industry ever, and the states agreed to drop a large portion of their claims. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Twenty-nine US states are seeking huge damages, claiming Meta’s platforms were addictive by design

In 1994, more than 40 US states came together to sue one of the most powerful industries on Earth: big tobacco.

Thirty years later, smoking is on the rise in the developing world, the companies involved remain profitable and the global tobacco market is worth nearly $1tn.

On Tuesday a major trial against Meta began, in which 29 states have brought the claim that the parent of Facebook and Instagram designed a deliberately addictive product and targeted it at children.

That trial follows a bellwether case earlier this year, in which a Los Angeles jury found the social media company – and YouTube, its co-defendant – liable for deliberately designing an addictive product that had deleterious effects on the mental health of a single young claimant.

That case, which awarded the claimant $6m, opened the door for this and other litigation. At about the same time, Meta was forced to pay a total of $942m in a separate trial in New Mexico. The New Mexico case focused on whether the company was aware of – and took measures to prevent – child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

This next wave of litigation will focus less on child exploitation, and more on the fundamental design of Meta’s platform: the algorithm that underlies which content it shows to users and how. So, how far could the litigation go?

Kate Winick, an analyst at Forrester, said the trial was “potentially the end of social media as we know it” and, while a ruling against Meta would not permanently kill the industry, it could “significantly reduce usage over the long term”.

The figures that Meta and other social media companies could stand to pay are immense. The attorneys general are seeking $200bn in damages, the amount of revenue the company takes in a year. Meta has said in a court filing that they could amount to $1.4tn, which is just short of the company’s market capitalisation. The judge in the case has called the company’s estimation “unreasonable”.

It is this algorithm that American attorneys general seem interested in changing, because it is this “dopamine-manipulating” feature – in the words of the AGs’ lawsuit – that makes social media addictive. Changes to this algorithm may not alter how Facebook advertises, said Steven Murdoch, a professor at University College London. But it could reduce engagement, which could gravely reduce its opportunity to advertise to users.

But all this depends on how big of a swing a US jury – and US regulators – are willing to take at the platform. Discontent is brewing worldwide about Meta and its business; the EU also wants the company to modify its “addictive design”.

“There’s a plausible path” for global changes to the algorithm, said Murdoch. “But whether it’s devastating or not – I’m not convinced the things that are plausibly going to be asked for are going to be devastating for the company.”

Take the recent case of Google. US regulators sued the search company in 2023 in a landmark antitrust case – which could have ended with authorities breaking up the company, perhaps forcing it to sell Chrome, the most popular web browser in the world. Google lost the case but that extreme penalty wasn’t imposed . Despite finding that the company had engaged in monopolistic practices, it got away with what critics called a “ slap on the wrist ” and remains a juggernaut.

“I don’t think anyone really wants to destroy Facebook. It’s a valuable company and there would be so many bad outcomes,” said Murdoch.

A Meta spokesperson said: “The state AGs may call this a landmark case but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate.

“Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. We stand by our record of creating strong protections for teens, and look forward to making our case in court.”

In 1994, more than 40 US states came together to sue one of the most powerful industries on Earth: big tobacco.
Thirty years later, smoking is on the rise in the developing world, the companies involved remain profitable and the global tobacco market is worth nearly $1tn.
On Tuesday a major trial against Meta began, in which 29 states have brought the claim that the parent of Facebook and Instagram designed a deliberately addictive product and targeted it at children.

That trial follows a bellwether case earlier this year, in which a Los Angeles jury found the social media company – and YouTube, its co-defendant – liable for deliberately designing an addictive product that had deleterious effects on the mental health of a single young claimant.

That case, which awarded the claimant $6m, opened the door for this and other litigation. At about the same time, Meta was forced to pay a total of $942m in a separate trial in New Mexico. The New Mexico case focused on whether the company was aware of – and took measures to prevent – child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

This next wave of litigation will focus less on child exploitation, and more on the fundamental design of Meta’s platform: the algorithm that underlies which content it shows to users and how. So, how far could the litigation go?

Kate Winick, an analyst at Forrester, said the trial was “potentially the end of social media as we know it” and, while a ruling against Meta would not permanently kill the industry, it could “significantly reduce usage over the long term”.

Meta has said in a court filing that they could amount to $1.4tn, which is just short of the company’s market capitalisation.
